methods: Pair comparisons required both activities to be present at the first interview. The pair and each single activity were compared with none stopped. Direct contrasts divide the pair risk ratio by the risk ratio for the stated constituent. Models for all cohorts and outside HRS use a common exposure coefficient with cohort-specific covariate coefficients and participant-clustered variance. These intervals omit between-cohort variation. Counts in parentheses denote deaths or new ADL limitations. No pair met the requirements for random-effects synthesis. The last column gives events per model parameter for pair rows and the safeguarded pooled risk ratio for rows omitting an activity. The drinking-plus-paid-work comparison and the work-containing comparisons outside HRS have limited model event support. Rows omitting an activity keep the original analysis population and count activities stopped among the remaining activities, with none stopped among those activities as reference.

methods: Activities started were absent at the first interview and present at the second. The four combinations compare started only, stopped only, and both stopped and started with neither. Direct comparisons of started versus none started among person-intervals with one activity stopped were repeated in participants able to start an initially absent activity. These models used the primary covariates, then indicators for which activity stopped or the combination of initial engagement pattern and activity stopped. In these rows the comparison group started an activity and the reference group did not. Both groups had one activity stopped unless stated otherwise. One-stage intervals describe within-sample uncertainty. Random-effects intervals use the Hartung–Knapp safeguard. Unavailable comparisons had insufficient group support and are not assigned a null estimate.

title: Pre-window health changes under both adjustment specifications
footnotes: A, lighter adjustment; B, full adjustment; ADL, activities of daily living; IADL, instrumental activities of daily living; SD, standard deviation. CI, confidence interval; RR, risk ratio; ELSA, English Longitudinal Study of Ageing; HRS, Health and Retirement Study; KLoSA, Korean Longitudinal Study of Ageing; SHARE, Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe.
methods: Pre-window changes occurred between an earlier interview and the first interview. Specification A included age, sex, interview wave, education, income, and the preceding level of the health measure. Fully adjusted specification B also included the initial number of activities, smoking, and diagnosed-condition count. The table reports risk ratios for binary measures and adjusted mean differences in cohort-specific standard-deviation units for depressive change. Both estimates and counts refer to the stated specification. Pooled rows include only evaluable cohorts and use safeguarded Hartung–Knapp intervals. Hospitalization was not pooled because recall periods differ. IADL increase had fewer than three evaluable cohorts.

footnotes: CI, confidence interval; RR, risk ratio; ELSA, English Longitudinal Study of Ageing; HRS, Health and Retirement Study; KLoSA, Korean Longitudinal Study of Ageing; SHARE, Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe. All risk ratios use none stopped as reference.
methods: Stable measured prior health required stable or improved self-rated health and no ADL limitation at the first interview, with both measures observed at the earlier and first interviews. All death models used the main covariate specification. Delayed analyses excluded undated deaths and conditioned on survival beyond the stated time after the second interview. No delay uses the same dated-death population. Events on or before the specified month were excluded. Unsupported groups were removed from the fitted model. The model counts therefore can differ from all eligible person-intervals. Summary estimates use random-effects pooling with safeguarded Hartung–Knapp intervals when three cohorts contribute. The two-cohort estimates use fixed-effect pooling, as labeled. ELSA had no month-resolved death dates. The completeness rows show dated deaths divided by total deaths in the primary risk set.
